Auditing Grasp Feasibility Predictors with Planner-Verified Counterfactuals

Sajid Ansari Affiliation: IIIT Hyderabad, India    Antony Thomas Affiliation: IIIT Hyderabad, India    Girish Varma Affiliation: IIIT Hyderabad, India
Abstract

Grasp-feasibility predictors report near-perfect accuracy on Task and Motion Planning benchmarks, but high accuracy on these benchmarks does not verify that a predictor uses the collision geometry that the motion planner checks. We propose a planner-verified counterfactual (CF) test: holding the grasp pose fixed, we insert a solid obstacle into the approach corridor, add its points to the model input, and let a planner re-derive the label, which flips from feasible to infeasible. Across eight predictors spanning point clouds, voxels, depth, and object tokens, CF-pair AUROC falls from high natural AUROC (0.9200.920–0.9960.996) to chance (0.4700.470–0.5040.504), and the flip holds across four planners, two arms, and a real-object obstacle. Predictors fail at different resolutions, from a bounding box to a 12.512.5 cm voxel. In the point-cloud models we dissect, the obstacle either moves the representation in a direction unrelated to whether it blocks the grasp or is not registered at all. A clearance-aware read of the corridor points, trained on the unmodified benchmark with no counterfactual scenes, reaches 0.9830.983 CF-pair AUROC, but it remains bound to its trained obstacle placements; a placement-invariant clearance representation is still open. We release the counterfactual labels, metrics, datasheet, and relabeling pipeline at https://github.com/codewithsajid/graspfc-cf.

1 Introduction

Computing grasp poses (grasps) is a fundamental problem in robotic manipulation. Given a grasp on an object, the end-effector can reach it only if a collision-free path exists from the robot’s start configuration; motion planning is feasible when such a path exists and infeasible otherwise. Sampling-based planners [18] commonly used in manipulation are only probabilistically complete, so they cannot certify infeasibility: they keep searching until termination or timeout, inflating overall computation time.

Learned predictors [4, 7, 6, 1, 2] that score this feasibility from a scene are now a standard speed-up for Task and Motion Planning (TAMP) [17, 6, 13, 29], and on point-cloud benchmarks they report near-perfect accuracy.11 1 TAMP combines discrete actions of task planning with the continuous geometric motion planning. A task-level action may turn out to be infeasible at the motion-level, e.g., objects obstructing a grasp, requiring task-level re-planning. However, these benchmarks evaluate predictor models on naturally sampled grasps, for which the grasp pose is often sufficient to predict the label. A predictor can therefore saturate the benchmark without using the full scene geometry checked by the motion planner. Fig. 1 shows one such grasp: the initial feasible grasp (left) is made infeasible by inserting the cube (right), yet the predictor’s feasibility score remains unchanged.

Collisions are a frequent and significant source of grasp infeasibility (Sec. 3). A natural question is why standard benchmarks fail to reveal collision. Their sampling rarely includes examples near the boundary where a small change in geometry causes a grasp to switch from feasible to infeasible (Sec. 4.1). Consequently, high accuracy on the benchmark does not verify that the model reasons about collisions. The model can achieve high accuracy without actually learning this aspect of grasp feasibility. This exposes two related issues: shortcut learning [16] and causal confusion [7], both of which can be measured directly through controlled interventions.

We evaluate different models using their released weights on their original benchmarks and robots. The models do not fail in the same way. Instead, each responds only at the level of detail its supervision, query formulation, and representation support, and stops below it (Sec. 4.3, Tab. 4). Importantly, the obstacle is present in the input representations. Thus, this insensitivity cannot simply be attributed to PointNet’s critical-point-set theorem [25], which concerns the learned per-point representation rather than the geometric structure of the scene. We verify this directly in Sec. 4.4. Further evidence comes from a clearance-supervised model trained on the same unmodified benchmark, with no counterfactual data at all, which still recovers the collision term (Sec. 4.5).

Together, these results show that the relevant collision signal is present in the input, but standard supervision does not require the model to use it.

Contributions. We audit eight predictors: three classifiers of a grasp-feasibility benchmark [3] built on GraspNet-1B scenes [11], and five prior methods spanning point clouds, voxels, depth images, and object tokens [4, 7, 6, 1, 2]. For [3, 2, 4, 7], we additionally evaluate the authors’ released weights on their original data and robot platforms. These results leave open a fundamental question: do the predictors actually capture collision-relevant scene geometry? We introduce a systematic test, along with metrics and data, to measure this correspondence.

  • •

    Benchmark saturation and collision limits. Predictors that are near-perfect on the natural benchmark score 0.470.47-0.5040.504 once we insert an obstacle that flips the collision label at the same grasp (Sec. 4.1, Tab. 1). Natural data almost never places two grasps at the same pose on opposite sides of a contact boundary, so a predictor can score well without reading the scene (Sec. 4.1).

  • •

    Planner-verified counterfactual test and metrics. We define the corridor insertion edit and verify both of its preconditions: every edit flips the planner’s label, and the inserted obstacle survives the model’s downsampling (Sec. 3). We report CF-pair and within-grasp AUROC, and release pick-clear accuracy for auditing new predictors. The planner-swap and real-object controls show the flip is not an artifact of one planner, arm, or obstacle type (Sec. 4.2).

  • •

    Predictors fall short in different ways. Each responds only down to the resolution its representation and supervision support, from a bounding box to a 12.512.5 cm voxel, with two point-cloud predictors not resolving the obstacle at all (Sec. 4.3, Tab. 4). Three do so on their authors’ own data and robot. We therefore report each at its own resolution rather than as one aggregate score.

  • •

    Collision signal in the input and supervised read. A clearance-supervised read of the same points reaches CF-pair 0.9830.983, trained on the unmodified benchmark and never shown a counterfactual scene (Sec. 4.5), consistent with ClearanceNet [20].

  • •

    A released counterfactual benchmark. Each label costs a planner call, so we release the GraspNet-1B counterfactual set with planner-verified labels, a datasheet [5], and the relabeling pipeline,22 2 Repository (code, data, and datasheet): https://github.com/codewithsajid/graspfc-cf. with each obstacle family as its own split. A new predictor can be scored on it without running a planner (supp. ).

2 Related Work

Learned grasp and motion feasibility. Predicting whether a grasp is reachable and collision-free is widely used to prune candidates before planning, where collision checking is the dominant runtime cost [36]. GraspNet-1B [11] provides real cluttered scenes and grasp annotations, atop a mature grasp-synthesis literature [24, 28]; a recent benchmark labels its grasps for motion feasibility with a planner [3]. Feasibility and collision predictors span point clouds, voxels, depth, and object tokens [4, 23, 7, 6, 1, 20, 2]. SceneCollisionNet [4] learns an implicit collision function for rearrangement, queried on a voxelized scene. PIGINet [7] scores the feasibility of a whole task-level plan from object tokens, and is never queried on a single approach corridor. NFC [6] and AGFP-Net [1] classify feasibility from depth for multi-robot manipulation planning. GRN [2] reasons over per-object bounding boxes and has an explicit obstruction head. Each reports high accuracy on its own benchmark, which we do not dispute. We ask a different question: does the benchmark test whether a predictor uses the collision geometry the motion planner checks?

Benchmark auditing, shortcut learning, and counterfactuals. Models that reach high accuracy through a spurious correlate rather than the intended signal, lead to recurring failure modes [16, 15]; additional inputs can make it worse, once it latches onto a non-causal cue [7]. Uninformed baselines and stress tests such as HANS [22] expose these shortcuts. Contrast sets [12] and counterfactually-augmented data [19] edit input minimally, then re-derive its label. Similar failures recur in 3D vision and robot learning, e.g., point-cloud networks latching onto rotation-frame cues [8]. Generalist policies generalize poorly when the bottleneck is dataset diversity rather than scale [33, 9]. Our test shows that an uninformed baseline model can succeed without the input and therefore may lead to wrong predictions when the input alone is changed; a motion planner, not a human annotator, certifies the new label.

Clearance as a supervised quantity. ClearanceNet [20] learns the clearance between a robot configuration and the scene, and uses the learned estimate to accelerate batched motion planning. Its lesson is that collision geometry is learnable once the query and the label are both stated in terms of clearance. A feasibility benchmark does not impose that condition. Its binary label supervises the outcome, not the geometric margin that produces it. We show the other half of that picture. Nothing in the benchmark forces a predictor to use the collision term, because a pose shortcut fits its labels just as well. The labels are still sufficient: supervising clearance over the same points, on the benchmark’s own splits, recovers the term (Sec. 4.5).

3D encoders and tokenizers. Point-cloud recognition is dominated by permutation-invariant encoders with max pooling [25] and their hierarchical [26, 27] and transformer [30] successors. PointNet’s critical-point-set theorem [25] is often read as making such encoders insensitive to added points. The condition is on the learned per-point map rather than on geometry, and it holds only for a single global max-pool with no local or positional branch. We measure it directly and find that the inserted points do move the pooled feature (Sec. 4.4). Self-supervised pretraining by masked reconstruction [37] or contrastive objectives [31] learns recognition features, which need not encode a contact boundary. Reconstruction tokenizers are the one case where the obstacle is lost outright (Sec. 4.4).

3 Counterfactual Methodology

The test requires four components: a fixed grasp, an insertable obstacle in the approach corridor, a planner to recompute the label, and a model input incorporating the obstacle points. With these in place, a single scene edit isolates the collision term while leaving all other factors unchanged. We evaluate on a shared benchmark and within each audited method’s native environment and robot (Sec. 4.3).

The shared benchmark and its oracle. The feasibility benchmark of [3] is built on GraspNet-1B [11]. It has 190190 real RGB-D tabletop scenes with official Seen, Similar, and Novel object splits. Each grasp carries a label from an RRT-Connect planner [21] oracle for a 7-DOF Franka Panda in PyBullet [4]. A grasp is feasible only when the planner finds a collision-free path to the pre-grasp pose (10 cm from grasp pose) from its home configuration. This gives 2,706,1602{,}706{,}160 per-grasp labels, 9.6%9.6\% of them feasible. The label is effectively deterministic: re-running the planner with 88 seeds on held-out grasps gives 0/4800/480 flips, so label noise is at most 0.6%0.6\% at 95%95\% confidence. The oracle is not the variable either. Labels do differ across planners and arms, so we vary both: four planning algorithms and two kinematic chains, the 7-DoF Panda and a 6-DoF xArm6. We call this the planner-swap control (Sec. 4.2, Tab. 3).

Collision decides most infeasibility. Across all labeled grasps, collision accounts for 64.3%64.3\% of infeasibility: 49.0%49.0\% from blocked transit and 15.3%15.3\% from blocked approach. The remaining 35.7%35.7\% is due to reachability. We assign each infeasible grasp to the first binding constraint in pipeline order, making these collision rates conservative lower bounds.

The edit. A perturbation is useful only if it changes the label and leaves a physically valid scene. We hold the grasp pose fixed, drop a solid box into the 1010 cm approach corridor, re-run the planner for the true new label, and add the box points to the model input (Fig. 2). We call this edit a corridor insertion. The box has edge 1.51.5 to 55 cm and sits at a 55 to 1515 cm standoff. Two properties are verified. First, the edit causes a real flip: it relabels every pair, while a matched box placed 3030 cm off-corridor leaves the grasp feasible 98.0%98.0\% of the time. Second, the obstacle survives downsampling, since every item retains at least one box point, ≈13\approx 13 on average, after farthest-point sampling to the 20482048-point input. A graded variant slides the box through six corridor offsets, from blocking to harmless, so a model must track where the obstacle is.

Obstacle families. The corridor box is the primary family, but we also vary the geometry, including spheres, non-convex L-shapes, table-mounted pillars, transit-path boxes, and four obstacle clusters. Size, standoff, and placement are independently swept, spanning six corridor offsets from blocking to harmless, plus adjacent, distal, and on-axis placements. A no-primitive family, the real-object control, uses a real benchmark object placed beside the target. Each family is planner-verified and released as a separate audit split (Sec. 4.2, Sec. 4.5, supp. ); geometry and the sampling details are specified in supp. .

Metrics. We report natural AUROC on the original splits without inserted obstacles. CF-pair AUROC ranks clear versus blocked versions of the same grasp at an identical pose, while within-grasp AUROC ranks feasible versus infeasible obstacle offsets. Chance is 0.50.5 for both. The audit suite additionally reports pick-clear accuracy: among two candidates where one is blocked, how often the clear grasp is ranked first (supp. ). Pose-only models cannot exceed chance on any metric, since paired examples share the same pose. CF-pair AUROC uses 1,0651{,}065 released pairs, with bootstrap 95%95\% CIs over pairs; trained results use 33 seeds. Thus, scores near 0.50.5 reflect genuine failure to detect collision, not estimation noise.

Models and evidence regimes. We evaluate three model groups (Tab. 1). (i) The three GraspFC classifiers of [3], run from their released weights on the shared benchmark. These are GraspFC-NNet, -Conv3D, and -PTX, the last on a PTv3 [30] backbone. (ii) Four prior representations, re-implemented and trained on the planner labels under one protocol: SceneCollisionNet, PIGINet, NFC [6], and AGFP-Net [1]. They share the oracle, the splits, and the loss, so this group tests the representation rather than the authors’ deployed system. (iii) Released weights of published methods run on their own data (Sec. 4.3). Per-model architectures and losses are in supp. . Every label on the shared benchmark comes from the same RRT-Connect oracle, which we verify deterministic and causal (supp. ).

4 Experiments

4.1 Benchmark saturation and collision sensitivity

Tab. 1 reports the audited predictors. All are near-perfect on the natural benchmark, but this score does not distinguish predictors that use collision geometry from those that do not. On same-pose counterfactuals, every predictor scores 0.470.47-0.5040.504 AUROC (within-grasp 0.470.47 to 0.520.52). GRN is the one predictor whose score changes at all, and only to obstacle presence: it cannot resolve the sub-bounding-box shape that determines collision (Fig. 6), so its entry (∗) is a shape swap rather than an insertion. This failure is not due to input modality. The obstacle appears in the voxel grid of GraspFC-Conv3D and in all five depth views of AGFP-Net, yet both discard it; NFC uses only the grasp pose and never its neighbor channel (Tab. 4). The deciding geometry is therefore present in the inputs and can be recovered from the same points (Sec. 4.5).

Why natural labels do not require collision. Feasibility labels are geometrically separated, with labels flipping at contact boundaries that natural sampling rarely straddles, making same-pose contrast essentially absent. Conditioning on grasp difficulty, which carries no scene information, therefore removes most of the model’s apparent advantage. This matches the benchmark’s own observation that grasp pose rather than scene geometry carries the feasibility signal [3]. The input holds the collision geometry, as shown in Sec. 4.5, recovering it under the benchmark’s own labels. The label distribution never requires a predictor to use it, so no quantity of natural data forces the term into the model. This follows from how the labels distribute, not from one benchmark’s design.

4.2 Robustness to placement, obstacle, planner, and robot

The result is not an artifact of our re-implementations or of one obstacle location. Re-scoring inference-only, with no model seeing a new label, we move the obstacle to held-out scenes and unseen placements. These are an adjacent in-crop offset (CF-adjacent, n=561n=561) and a distal out-of-crop offset (CF-distal, n=250n=250). Every model stays in [0.47,0.554][0.47,0.554] at every placement, and its score barely moves with or without the obstacle (Tab. 2). Fig. 3 shows the dual fact for the cured models, those we fine-tune or train on planner-relabeled counterfactual pairs. Counterfactual training makes them react only within a shell around the gripper. No model we test, cured or not, holds a clearance representation that survives moving the obstacle across the workspace. The result also holds across standoff and obstacle type, shown below, and across dense multi-object clutter (supp. ). Most tellingly, it holds in the real-object control, where the obstacle is not a foreign primitive at all: a GraspNet-1B object from the same Novel split, resting on the table next to the target, flips every one of 150150 grasps, while a matched copy set aside leaves all of them feasible. The deployed model returns essentially the same score either way (|Δ​p|=0.001|\Delta p|=0.001; Tab. 3, supp. ). The diagnosis is therefore not an out-of-distribution obstacle artifact.

Oracle, obstacle type, and embodiment. We re-run the planner-verified counterfactual under three standoffs and two further obstacle types, and with an in-distribution dataset object from the test splits placed in the grasp approach direction (supp. ). The deployed model is re-scored on each (Tab. 3). The resting case is gravity-plausible: a pillar standing on the table that rises into the descent corridor, not a floating body. The third case lies in the arm’s transit path, the dominant 49.0%49.0\% blocked-transit failure mode. The edits therefore span both feasibility terms and are physically realizable. In every variant the planner relabels the grasp, with causal flip 0.560.56 to 1.001.00, while a matched off-corridor null box leaves it feasible ≥97%\geq 97\% of the time. The deployed model stays near chance throughout (CF-pair AUROC 0.4910.491 to 0.5000.500) and returns an essentially identical score with and without the obstacle (|Δ​p|≤0.001|\Delta p|\leq 0.001). Dense clutter behaves the same: a cluster of four obstacles flips all 150150 re-checked grasps, and the model stays at chance (CF-pair 0.4980.498, |Δ​p|<0.001|\Delta p|<0.001; supp. ).

The oracle itself is not the variable either. The planner-swap control relabels the grasp in 88 of 88 conditions at flip rate 1.0001.000 (Tab. 3). The diagnosis therefore tracks the representation, not the standoff, the obstacle shape, the planning algorithm, or the arm.

4.3 Released weights on the authors’ own data

Most directly, we run published models from their own released weights on their own benchmarks (Tabs. 4, 4, 5 and 6), which removes the re-implementation caveat. The verdicts are not uniform. Each model responds at the resolution its supervision, native query semantics, and representation provide, and stops responding below it (Tab. 4). PIGINet, on its authors’ PR2 kitchen, calls a planner-blocked pick feasible 90%90\% of the time against a ground truth of 0%0\% (Fig. 4; aggregated in supp. ). It is a sequence-level predictor over object tokens and was never queried on an approach corridor, and the shortcut extends to multi-step plans (supp. ). SceneCollisionNet, on its own ACRONYM [10] scenes, is the one audited predictor that responds to shape above chance (0.8210.821 on a same-bounding-box swap). It is not a decision boundary. Swept from a deep overlap to a 66 cm clear gap, its score holds at pcoll=0.76p_{\mathrm{coll}}=0.76 straight across the true contact boundary (Fig. 5). It reads contact, and stops at its 12.512.5 cm voxel (supp. ). GRN reads a bounding box by design. It detects inserted geometry, yet scores a box and its inscribed same-bounding-box ellipsoid identically: a shape-swap AUROC of 0.5000.500, with two further geometry holes in supp. . One aggregate number over these predictors would hide five mechanisms with five different remedies.

4.4 Where the collision term is lost

If the deciding evidence is in the input, where is it lost? Not at the pooling step, and not by construction. PointNet’s critical-point-set theorem [25] does not say that points inside a critical set’s hull cannot change the global feature. It gives a critical set and an upper-bound set, and adding points leaves the pooled feature unchanged exactly when no added point raises a pooled channel. That is a condition on the learned per-point map, not on geometry. We measure it on GraspFC-NNet’s max-pooled branch in isolation, over the planner-verified pairs, and the condition fails. Only 16%16\% of the inserted points raise no channel, and the obstacle raises 31.531.5 of 256256 channels. The pooled feature moves more than a mean pool would move it (0.1740.174 against 0.0990.099), because the inserted points are extremal.

The obstacle therefore enters the representation. Decomposing the deployed forward pass shows how far it gets. Inside the full model that same max-pooled branch moves by 0.0740.074 and the scene branch by 0.2120.212. The head is not frozen either, with a per-pair |Δ​logit||\Delta\text{logit}| of 0.3650.365. What the movement lacks is sign. The mean Δ​logit\Delta\text{logit} is only +0.017+0.017, and the alignment between the feature displacement and the one direction the head can read has mean cosine +0.043+0.043 against a magnitude of 0.2510.251. The response is large and direction-random. We test this directly by placing two obstacles at the identical grasp pose, adding the same number of points to the same cloud, one blocking the approach and one 3030 cm off-corridor. GraspFC-NNet registers both strongly (|Δ​p||\Delta p| 0.0270.027) and GraspFC-PTX registers neither (0.0010.001). Neither ranks the blocking one below the harmless one (blocking AUROC 0.4810.481 and 0.5020.502, bootstrap intervals containing 0.50.5). These are two different failures with two different fixes.

Nor is the cause the weights (Tab. 5). Neither recognition-pretrained encoders (PointNet++ [26], PointNeXt-S [27]) nor the deployed model’s own feasibility-trained PTv3 [30] lets clearance be linearly read from its features. Only an explicit clearance tokenization of the same points does. Pretraining is irrelevant: GraspFC-PTX is near-perfect on the natural benchmark yet at 0.4980.498 CF-pair, whether trained from scratch or from Sonata self-supervised weights [31]. Reconstruction does not help either. The deciding obstacle is a small fraction of the points, so a Point-BERT-style autoencoder [37] discards most of it on encoding. Nothing in the natural supervision ever required the score to move in the right direction, which is the sense in which the term is not extracted. Clearance supervision changes that (Sec. 4.5).

4.5 What does not close the gap, and what does

Nothing on the natural benchmark closes the gap (Tab. 6). Scaling natural data does nothing. Fine-tuning the deployed model on counterfactuals does not transfer across five standard recipes, and width is not the lever either, since a 10×10\times wider encoder tracks the baseline. The shortcut is imprinted in the pretrained weights. The obvious escape is to retrain the same architecture from scratch on counterfactual labels. That does raise the in-distribution counterfactual score (CF-pair 0.9910.991), which alone shows the limit is not representational in principle. But it is fitting the intervention rather than learning clearance. The cured model is placement-bound, and its score falls back toward chance the moment the obstacle leaves the trained corridor (Fig. 3), so retraining on a new placement only fits a new shortcut. Counterfactual data buys coverage of the trained obstacle distribution, not a transferable collision representation. The lever is the representation, which we turn to next.

Clearance supervision on the unmodified benchmark. Concretely, the collision term can be learned at train time from the unmodified benchmark alone, with no counterfactual scenes, by exposing its geometric signal (corridor clearance) to the network. Fig. 7 shows the ladder, all trained on the original splits with plain BCE. A pose representation stays at chance (CF-pair 0.5030.503). Raw corridor points recover part of the term (0.8430.843). A clearance-aware tokenization of the same points reaches CF-pair 0.9830.983 with only 2323k parameters, beating a param-free geometric readout of those tokens (0.900.90). The tokenization slices the 1010 cm corridor into K=13K{=}13 axial slabs (supp. ). This model is trained on the unmodified benchmark, and is distinct from the from-scratch 0.9910.991 of Tab. 6, which trains on counterfactual data. Two further train-time changes sharpen it on the same data: a per-point clearance channel, and a soft-min over per-region clearances that makes the predictor monotone by construction (supp. ). Two models tied on the benchmark thus separate under the protocol on no new data. The separation comes from a learned read of the clearance tokens, not an analytic check bolted onto the output. This is a diagnostic, not a deployable predictor. Like the from-scratch cure it still degrades off the trained placement distribution, as we show next, so a clearance representation that generalizes across placement (supp. ) is future work.

Transfer to unseen obstacle shapes and placements. The hostile reading is that a counterfactual-cured model merely memorized our obstacle generator. It did not: trained on box counterfactuals and evaluated, planner-relabeled, on never-seen spheres, the cure transfers at or above its in-distribution score, while a no-cloud control stays at chance. It also holds on a never-seen non-convex L-shape and transfers, more weakly, to an unseen on-axis placement family, in every case far above chance. The cure computes occupancy from the points, so it transfers across held-out obstacle shape and, more weakly, placement, rather than memorizing one generator. Per-architecture scores and bootstrap CIs are in Fig. 8.

5 Discussion and Conclusion

We audit grasp-feasibility predictors with the corridor insertion: a planner-verified counterfactual edit that holds the grasp pose fixed, places a solid obstacle in the approach corridor, and enters its points into the model input. It flips the label on every pair and survives the model’s downsampling. Collision decides 64.3%64.3\% of infeasibility, but predictors with near-perfect natural AUROC score 0.470.47 to 0.5040.504 on the counterfactual pairs. The obstacle does reach the representation: in GraspFC-NNet its scene feature moves by 21%21\%. The score still does not change with whether the obstacle blocks. The natural distribution almost never contains the fixed-pose contrast that would require it to (Sec. 4.1). The input carries the collision term, and the benchmark does not identify it.

The failure is not uniform. GRN reads a bounding box, SceneCollisionNet a 12.512.5 cm voxel, GraspFC-NNet registers the obstacle but cannot say whether it blocks, and GraspFC-PTX, the deployed model, does not register it at all (|Δ​p|≈0.001|\Delta p|\approx 0.001). Each fails below its own resolution. This holds across placement, dense clutter, the real-object control, and every planner-swap condition. Clearance supervision closes the gap: the benchmark’s own labels are sufficient, and a 2323k-parameter read of corridor clearance reaches CF-pair 0.9830.983 (Sec. 4.5), while training on the interventions instead only fits them. That read stays bound to its trained placement distribution, and we evaluate in simulation with a sampling-based planner as oracle. We release the pairs, metrics, datasheet, and pipeline, so new predictors can be audited without a planner call (supp. ). Generalizing a clearance representation across obstacle placement remains an open problem.

Auditing Grasp Feasibility Predictors with Planner-Verified Counterfactuals

[main.pdf]

\thetitle

Supplementary Material

Roadmap. We first give the robustness figures (oracle standoff, obstacle type, a dataset object, and dense clutter) and the physical cost of the result; Appendix A then extends the protocol to multi-step plan feasibility; Appendix B gives the shape- and contact-resolution detail for GRN and SceneCollisionNet on their own benchmarks; Appendix C lists per-model architecture, training pool, and in-distribution accuracy; Appendix D gives the per-model interventional scores and the representation-to-failure taxonomy; Appendix E dissects why GRN partially passes; Appendix F reports the negative controls and label-integrity checks; Appendix G specifies the clearance-aware tokenization; and Appendices H and I provide the datasheet and the audit protocol for the released benchmark.

Robustness of the diagnosis: figures and the physical cost

The main paper establishes that the diagnosis survives the oracle standoff, the obstacle type, the planner, and the arm (). Here we give the figures behind that result, the per-condition planner-swap scores, a worked example, dense clutter, and the downstream cost of the result.

A worked example.

in the main paper shows one such instance in full: a single grasp on a GraspNet-1B scene under all four conditions. Tab. 8 reports its per-condition scores. The three obstacles trigger two distinct geometric failure modes (a blocked approach for the corridor box and the resting pillar, a blocked transit for the path box), and the deployed SOTA returns the same p⁡(feasible)p(\text{feasible}) to within 0.0010.001 across all four, although the planner flips three of them. This is not a hand-selected pair: it is one of the instances counted in , where the planner flipped every obstacle type while the model never moved.

Dense multi-object clutter.

The diagnosis also survives dense clutter rather than a single inserted body. Inserting a cluster of four solid obstacles into the approach flips all 150150 test grasps the planner re-checks (causal flip 1.001.00, across two failure modes: 149149 blocked-approach and 11 blocked-transit), yet the deployed SOTA returns the same p⁡(feasible)p(\text{feasible}) with and without the cluster (CF-pair AUROC 0.4980.498, |Δ​p|<0.001|\Delta p|<0.001); Fig. 12 shows one example.

The result has a physical cost.

The score gap is not only a ranking artifact; it changes what a robot does. On one counterfactual scene (Novel split, scene 160160) we execute the candidate grasps in physics simulation (Fig. 13). The pose-shortcut model’s top-ranked grasp, the one it scores feasible, drives the gripper into the inserted corridor box, a pybullet-verified contact. Screening the same 2020 candidate grasps with the clearance-aware read of instead returns a top-1 whose approach is collision-free, verified by a BiRRT path. This is one scene, illustrating the score’s downstream effect, not a deployment claim. Same scene, same candidates: the deciding difference is whether the score reads the geometry the planner checks.

Appendix A The protocol extends to multi-step plan feasibility

Single-grasp feasibility is one action; many planners predict feasibility for a whole action sequence. Our protocol applies unchanged (Fig. 15): insert an obstacle, re-run the oracle on the edited state, and relabel each step and the suffix it gates. Two points make this concrete. (i) PIGINet [7], one of the audited models, is itself a sequence-based plan-feasibility predictor; run from its released weights on its authors’ own PR2 kitchen it calls a planner-blocked plan feasible 90%90\% of the time (Fig. 14; , ), so the shortcut is already demonstrated on a multi-step predictor, not only on single-grasp classifiers. (ii) Our release includes a whole-skeleton feasibility generator that carries symbolic preconditions and accumulated geometric state across kk steps, so the same insert-and-relabel protocol extends to sequences with no change to the metric.

Appendix B Shape and contact resolution on the methods’ own data

shows the recreated GRN scene in the main paper; here we give the quantitative detail of the two released-weights results that are easiest to misread, and the recreated SceneCollisionNet scenes (). GRN detects an inserted obstacle on its panda_3d_4 benchmark (feasibility 0.990.99 clear, 0.940.94 beside, 0.010.01 on-path), but a box and its inscribed same-bounding-box ellipsoid receive an identical score, so the shape-swap AUROC is exactly 0.5000.500 and shape is decisive for 14%14\% of configurations (Fig. 16): GRN reads the bounding box, not the shape. SceneCollisionNet, run from the released checkpoint on an ACRONYM-style cluttered tabletop in its trained workspace, does not resolve its own contact boundary: as a gripper-held cube is swept against a solid obstacle from overlapping it to a 66 cm clear gap (), the released score stays pinned at pcoll=0.76p_{\mathrm{coll}}=0.76 (full-sweep range 0.750.75 to 0.770.77, never below 0.50.5), scoring a deep collision and a 66 cm clearance identically where an ideal checker steps from 11 to 00. At its 12.512.5 cm voxel it is geometry-agnostic below the cell size: in controlled box probes it registers gross presence (removing the obstacle drops the score 0.670.67 to 0.120.12) but resolves shape only weakly (same-bounding-box shape swap, 0.8210.821 AUROC, not a decision boundary). The common factor across all three released-weights systems is geometry-agnosticism below each representation’s resolution.

Appendix C Per-model training and architecture

Every re-implemented predictor is trained on the same GraspNet-1B planner labels under one protocol (shared oracle, splits, and a binary-cross-entropy objective); the three GraspFC classifiers are the feasibility predictors of [3], and GRN is run from released weights on its own data. Tab. 9 gives each model’s representation, training pool, and in-distribution accuracy, so a reader can see that the interventional gap of is not an under-training artifact: every model reaches high in-distribution AUROC on the same labels before its score falls under the intervention. Class balance is the benchmark’s natural 24.1%24.1\% feasible on the 100-scene training split (the full label pool is 9.6%9.6\% feasible); PIGINet’s kitchen pool is 69%69\% feasible, close to the authors’ own 67%67\%. The three GraspFC classifiers share one recipe (binary cross-entropy with logits, positive weight 3.143.14, AdamW at 1.5×10−31.5{\times}10^{-3} with cosine decay, 3030 epochs, batch 128128) on the benchmark’s 100100-scene, 1.521.52M-grasp training split; each re-implementation follows its own paper’s loss, noted in Tab. 9.

Appendix D Per-model interventional results and the representation-to-failure taxonomy

reports natural and CF-pair AUROC; here we read it two ways. First, the representation-to-failure taxonomy (Tab. 10) names, for each model, the coarsest collision geometry its representation resolves and the mechanism behind the gap; the single common axis is that each model is geometry-agnostic below its representation’s resolution. Second, the behavioral gallery (Tab. 11) gives the score each model returns with and without the flip-causing obstacle on a matched set: five predictors return essentially the clear-scene score (|Δ​p|≤0.02|\Delta p|\leq 0.02) while the planner flips the label, and GRN, the one model with a supervised obstruction head fed the box, moves with the planner. The obstacle is verified present in every model’s input (it renders into NFC’s dedicated neighbor channel, into all five of AGFP-Net’s depth views, and, for the deployed SOTA, a frame audit re-places it on the approach corridor in the model’s own input frame; Appendix F), so a flat score is the representation discarding visible evidence, not a missing input.

Appendix E Why GRN partially passes, and where it does not

GRN is the one audited model that reacts to an inserted obstacle, so it deserves a careful reading: it is neither a counterexample to the diagnosis nor a solved case. The difference is structural. GRN has an explicit, supervised, factored grasp-obstruction head that is fed each object’s box and pose, which the monolithic predictors lack, and on the two things that head can express it is causally faithful. (i) Presence. Removing the true obstructor flips GRN to feasible 94/91/90%94/91/90\% of the time across 4/10/204/10/20-object scenes, while removing a random non-obstructor flips it 0%0\%, ruling out an any-edge-removal artifact. On the same insertion probe we apply to the other models, GRN scores clear versus blocked AUROC 1.0001.000 (p​ 0.990→0.007p\,0.990\to 0.007; a beside control stays at 0.9430.943): the same probe that leaves the other models at chance moves GRN end to end. Instrumenting GRN’s graph construction confirms the inserted node enters the computation and its obstruction head fires proportionally to geometry (1.001.00 in the approach versus 0.280.28 beside), so the discriminator is the head’s reasoning, not mere edge presence. (ii) Bounding-box clearance. Shrinking or sliding the obstacle moves GRN’s score smoothly and monotonically, crossing 0.50.5 right as the boxes separate; it tracks clearance magnitude, not just presence, at the bounding-box level.

Where it fails is below that representation. GRN’s per-object input is an axis-aligned box plus yaw, with no shape and no out-of-plane pose, so any geometry the box cannot encode is invisible by construction, and the failures span both error directions (Tab. 12). A solid box and its inscribed same-bounding-box ellipsoid receive an identical prediction, yet 14%14\% of configurations are shape-decisive (the box intersects the approach corridor while the ellipsoid does not), giving a shape-swap AUROC of exactly 0.5000.500. A center-fixed obstacle tilted into the approach is identical to the same object standing upright, because pitch and roll are dropped at the node, so on 72.5%72.5\% of these tilted-obstacle cases GRN reads the object as upright and commands a colliding grasp: a false-clear, the unsafe direction. An open frame or bin is filled to its solid bounding box, so GRN abandons a reachable grasp 100%100\% of the time: a false-block. Each is a matched pair GRN scores identically while true feasibility flips, so its AUROC is chance on all three against an oracle’s 1.01.0.

For a datasets venue, these geometries are out of GRN’s box-only benchmark distribution, and that is the point: GRN’s high score on its own benchmark is partly due to the benchmark’s limited geometry (axis-aligned boxes), and the counterfactuals expose the failures the dataset hides. This is a dataset-and-representation critique, not a claim that GRN is broken. (A practitioner could give GRN the recomputed bounding box of a tilted object, but that is external geometry GRN does not compute, and it would then over-block; the native representation assumes upright boxes.)

Appendix F Negative controls and label integrity

The diagnosis rests on the flip being caused by the true obstacle and on that obstacle being present in the model’s input, so we report the controls that close the obvious alternative explanations.

The obstacle is on the corridor in the model’s own frame. A concern is that the obstacle might float off the approach in the model’s input frame, which would make Δ​p≈0\Delta p\approx 0 a placement artifact. A frame audit re-places the box on the corridor in the deployed SOTA’s input frame and re-scores: the model still does not respond (clear-versus-box AUROC 0.498→0.5010.498\to 0.501, Δ​p≈0\Delta p\approx 0), so the result is not a misplacement artifact.

Flips are caused by the true obstructor, not any edit. A matched box placed 3030 cm off-corridor leaves the grasp feasible 98.0%98.0\% of the time, and the same holds for a box slid laterally off the finger axis (97%97\% feasible); for GRN, removing a random non-obstructor flips the label 0%0\% of the time versus 94%94\% for the true obstructor. The edits are causal and specific.

Non-diagnostic perturbations are excluded by design. A perturbation is only informative if the oracle relabels it. Naive cloud edits that do not change the label (50%50\% point dropout, 55 to 1010 mm jitter) move every model’s AUROC by 0.0000.000, which shows only that the model is insensitive to the cloud, not that it is wrong; we therefore never count them, and use only the insert-and-relabel intervention.

Labels are effectively deterministic. Re-running the planner with 88 seeds on held-out grasps gives 0/4800/480 flips (label noise ≤0.6%\leq 0.6\% at 95%95\% confidence), so the 0.990.99-level natural scores are not noise-limited.

The natural label is pose-recoverable, which is why natural data cannot supervise the term. A 2525-nearest-neighbor lookup on grasp pose alone, with no scene at all, scores 0.9630.963 natural AUROC on SceneCollisionNet’s task. The natural distribution carries the feasibility label in the pose, so a model is never forced to read the scene, which is the standing reason the counterfactual contrast is necessary rather than convenient.

The in-crop gap is representational, not an information limit. When the obstacle leaves the input crop (a distal control 3030 cm back), the cures fall to chance (raw 0.5170.517, clearance tokens 0.5050.505): an information limit, distinct from the in-crop case where the obstacle is present but discarded. The global-input cure (from-scratch on counterfactuals, full cloud) partially survives the distal move (0.6020.602, versus 0.4970.497 for the as-is deployed model, ), confirming the in-crop drop is about the representation, not the input.

Appendix G The clearance-aware tokenization (architecture and scope)

shows that the collision term, which no audited predictor resolves at the scale that decides the collision, is recoverable at train time from the original benchmark by a clearance-aware read of the grasp-local points. This appendix gives the construction behind that result (Fig. 17) and states what it does and does not establish. It is a diagnostic: it isolates where the missing signal lives (the representation), not a deployable collision predictor. The distinction matters because, as shows, a learned read of these tokens is still placement-bound, like the from-scratch counterfactual cure.

Tokenization.

We work in the gripper frame, where collision is exactly SE(3)-invariant (the obstacle’s gripper-frame coordinates are unchanged by any rigid motion of the scene-plus-grasp). We slice the 1010 cm approach corridor into K=13K=13 axial slabs along the approach axis aa. Each non-target scene point is projected onto aa to get an axial coordinate zz and a lateral radius ρ\rho (its perpendicular distance from the approach line); points outside the corridor extent are dropped. Slab kk emits a three-number token [ρk,occk,zk][\,\rho_{k},\,\mathrm{occ}_{k},\,z_{k}\,]: ρk\rho_{k} is the minimum lateral clearance of any obstacle point in that slab (capped), occk\mathrm{occ}_{k} is its occupancy (a soft point count), and zkz_{k} is the slab center. The result is a fixed K×3K\times 3 tensor regardless of how many points fall in the corridor, so the representation is point-count-agnostic and obstacle-localizing by construction: the channel ρk\rho_{k} is a direct readout of where the swept gripper comes closest to matter, the very quantity the planner checks.

Network.

A shared per-slab MLP (→323\!\to\!32, GELU) maps each token to an embedding; we max-pool over slabs and append the two global statistics mink⁡ρk\min_{k}\rho_{k} and maxk⁡occk\max_{k}\mathrm{occ}_{k}, then a small collision MLP produces a clearance feature hCh_{C}. A separate pose head produces hRh_{R} from the same 1717-dimensional pose descriptor the baselines use, and the two are concatenated into the final feasibility head. This is the R⊗CR\otimes C factorization of Fig. 17: hRh_{R} carries reachability (pose, not SE(3)-invariant) and hCh_{C} carries collision (gripper-frame, invariant). The whole network is 2323k parameters; the per-slab MLP is shared across slabs, so the parameter count is independent of KK (a sweep over K∈{5,9,13,21,31}K\in\{5,9,13,21,31\} leaves it at 22.822.8k and within-grasp AUROC at 0.9960.996 to 1.01.0).

Two readouts, one representation.

The point of the construction is that the collision signal is present in the tokens before any learning. Thresholding the single global statistic mink⁡ρk\min_{k}\rho_{k}, with no trained weights and no labels, already gives CF-pair AUROC 0.8990.899 and within-grasp 0.9110.911. The learned head on the identical tokens reaches CF-pair 0.9830.983. Learning therefore sharpens a signal the representation already exposes; it does not manufacture it. This is the central contrast: a pose representation cannot be made to read collision at any accuracy (, ), whereas a clearance representation makes the term readable at 0.900.90 with zero fitting. The gap is the representation, not learnability.

Two train-time innovations on the original data.

Two structural changes sharpen this clearance read on the original benchmark, with no counterfactual scenes, and are the constructions behind the “sharpen” claim of . (i) A per-point clearance channel. Appending each point’s corridor clearance to its input features raises a raw encoder’s clearance-probe R2R^{2} from 0.050.05 to 0.220.22; distilling the same signal into the pooled feature instead leaves it at 0.020.02, so the clearance must enter before pooling. (ii) A soft-min over per-region clearances. Replacing max-pooling with a soft-min over the per-slab clearances makes the feasibility head monotone in clearance by construction and cuts the insertion-monotonicity violation rate, the fraction of random point insertions that raise predicted feasibility, from 0.420.42 under max-pooling to 0.0250.025. Both act at train time on the original splits, so the collision term is sharpened without any counterfactual data.

What it does not establish.

The learned read is not a transferable collision model. Trained on one corridor placement it transfers across held-out obstacle shape and size in ranking (sphere, non-convex L, and 1.5/3/51.5/3/5 cm boxes all transfer at or above the in-distribution score), but its absolute calibration drifts under size shift and its accuracy falls on an unseen on-axis placement family (0.740.74, ), because workspace clearance equals configuration-space clearance only for a point robot. A transferable solution must learn a calibrated clearance field with the structural guarantees a binary classifier lacks (insertion-monotonicity, size transfer by Minkowski subtraction, and a certified screening bound); we treat that as the method that follows this dataset paper, not as a claim of the present work. Likewise, holding the Franka gripper fixed, varying only the finger aperture or the on-axis approach depth does not move the planner’s label (the arm body dominates the swept volume), so a true cross-gripper test needs a second arm and is out of scope here.

Out-of-distribution transfer of the cures.

gives the per-variant breakdown behind : three counterfactual-cured models (a generic architecture, a slab-tokenized model, and the clearance-token model), each trained on box counterfactuals and re-evaluated, planner-relabeled, on a held-out shape (sphere), placement (axial), and non-convex (L-shape) family. Every cure transfers at or near its in-distribution score; on the unseen on-axis placement the generic architecture transfers best (0.900.90) and the clearance one least (0.740.74), both far above chance, while the no-cloud control stays at 0.5000.500 throughout.

Appendix H Datasheet

This datasheet follows Gebru et al. [5].

Composition. The counterfactual benchmark pairs each base-feasible grasp with a planner-verified clear and obstacle-inserted variant at an identical pose, on public GraspNet-1B scenes. It includes the 1,0651{,}065 same-pose CF pairs used for CF-pair AUROC, graded obstacle-offset groups (one grasp with six offsets from blocking to harmless), and the held-out generalization and robustness sets used here: held-out shape (sphere), non-convex (L-shape), placement (axial), distal and adjacent placements, obstacle size (1.5/3/51.5/3/5 cm), standoff (5/10/155/10/15 cm), and the resting-pillar and transit-path obstacle types, plus the 150150 dataset-object pairs of Fig. 10 and the dense-clutter set of Fig. 12. Each instance stores the scene and grasp identifiers, the obstacle geometry and pose, the planner label, and the binding failure mode.

Collection and labels. Labels come from an RRT-Connect motion planner for a 7-DOF Franka Panda in PyBullet (IK at the grasp and a pre-grasp standoff, a collision-free linear approach, and a collision-free path from home). Each label is a fresh planner call on the edited scene (mean 2.512.51 s; median 2.372.37; n=40n=40). The label is effectively deterministic: re-running with 88 seeds on held-out grasps gives 0/4800/480 flips (label noise ≤0.6%\leq 0.6\% at 95%95\% confidence, rule of three).

Splits and intended use. Evaluation uses the official Seen/Similar/Novel object splits, with the counterfactual tests reported on Novel objects. Intended use is auditing obstacle-awareness of feasibility predictors. The protocol is also applied to three prior-work settings (SceneCollisionNet’s ACRONYM, PIGINet’s PR2 kitchen, GRN’s panda_3d_4) to show it is not tied to our data.

Responsible use, biases, and limitations. All labels are produced in simulation by a planner oracle; the benchmark is a diagnostic of obstacle-awareness and is not a deployment safety certificate, and a high score does not certify a model for use on a physical robot. The data inherit GraspNet-1B’s distribution (tabletop RGB-D scenes and its object set) and our single-arm Franka Panda setup, so coverage of arms, grippers, and environments is limited. By construction the natural feasibility label is largely recoverable from the grasp pose alone (Appendix F); this is the bias the counterfactual split is designed to expose rather than a defect to be corrected. Obstacles are geometrically inserted solid bodies validated by the planner relabel, not by physical settling.

Distribution and licensing. We release the planner-verified annotations, the obstacle geometry, the planner configuration, and the relabeling pipeline so others can score new models without re-running a planner and can regenerate labels for new obstacle families. The underlying RGB-D scenes remain under the GraspNet-1B license for research use, so we redistribute only the new annotations and code, not the source images. We release the new planner-verified annotations and this datasheet under CC BY 4.0 and the relabeling pipeline code under the MIT license. The annotations, datasheet, and relabeling pipeline are available at https://github.com/codewithsajid/graspfc-cf.

Maintenance, versioning, and contact. We will host the annotations, the pipeline, and a public leaderboard of interventional scores (Appendix I), version the release so scores remain comparable across updates, and document any errata or added obstacle families in a changelog.

Appendix I Using the released benchmark

The reusable contribution is that a model’s obstacle-awareness can be measured without a motion planner. To audit a new predictor MM: (1) load the released same-pose pairs; (2) for each pair, have MM score the clear cloud and the obstacle-inserted cloud at the identical grasp pose, adding the released obstacle points to MM’s input; (3) report CF-pair AUROC over the pairs, within-grasp AUROC over the graded-offset groups, and pick-clear accuracy. A model that reads only the grasp pose scores chance on all three by construction: on the released pairs the deployed SOTA and a pose-only baseline both score pick-clear 0.5000.500, exactly as on CF-pair, while a clearance-aware read of the same points reaches 0.9970.997 (raw corridor points recover part of it, 0.8170.817), so the metrics cannot be satisfied by a pose lookup. No planner call is needed at audit time: scoring the 1,0651{,}065-pair head-to-head set takes under a minute on one GPU, versus the ≈45\approx 45 minutes of planner time the labels themselves cost. Each obstacle family (shape, placement, size, standoff, resting, transit) is a separate split on which all three metrics are reported, so a submission can show which interventions a model survives. Regenerating labels for a new obstacle family is the only step that calls the planner, and the released pipeline does it from a single geometry specification. We will host the annotations, pipeline, and a public leaderboard of interventional scores.
